chunks.text: A function f is continuous at a point x = a if and only if three conditions all hold: f(a) is defined, lim(x→a) f(x) exists, and lim(x→a) f(x) equals f(a).
The first condition for continuity at x = a is that f(a) is defined, meaning the function actually has a value there and the graph shows a filled-in point rather than a hole.
The second condition for continuity at x = a is that lim(x→a) f(x) exists, which requires the left-hand limit and the right-hand limit to agree on a single value.

The third condition for continuity at x = a is that the limit equals the function value: lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a). This condition is the strongest because if it holds, the value and the limit must both exist.
The informal idea of continuity is that the graph can be drawn without lifting the pencil, but the precise definition requires the three-part test of value, limit, and their equality.

An existing limit alone does not guarantee continuity. A function can have a perfectly good limit at a point while still being discontinuous there because the value is undefined or does not match the limit.

A removable discontinuity occurs when the two-sided limit exists but the function value is either undefined or different from the limit. On a graph it appears as a single hole, sometimes with a stray dot elsewhere.

A removable discontinuity can be fixed by redefining the function's value at that point to equal the limit. For example, f(x) = (x² - 4)/(x - 2) has a removable discontinuity at x = 2 where the limit is 4 but f(2) is undefined.
A jump discontinuity occurs when both one-sided limits exist but are not equal to each other. On a graph the function breaks and jumps from one value to another, like a staircase step.
The greatest integer (floor) function has jump discontinuities at every integer. At x = 3 it jumps from a left-hand limit of 2 to a right-hand limit of 3.
An infinite discontinuity occurs when at least one one-sided limit is positive or negative infinity. The function blows up near the point, producing a vertical asymptote.
The function f(x) = 1/x has an infinite discontinuity at x = 0: as x approaches 0 from the right f(x) goes to positive infinity, and from the left it goes to negative infinity.

To classify a discontinuity: if the two-sided limit exists but the value is missing or misplaced it is removable; if one-sided limits exist but disagree it is a jump; if a one-sided limit is infinite it is infinite.

When a rational function is undefined at a point, factoring reveals the type: if the problematic factor cancels, the discontinuity is a removable hole; if it does not cancel and the denominator goes to zero, it is an infinite discontinuity.
Polynomials are continuous for all real numbers. Rational functions are continuous everywhere except where the denominator equals zero.

The square root function √x is continuous for x ≥ 0, sin x and cos x are continuous everywhere, eˣ is continuous everywhere, ln x is continuous for x > 0, and tan x is discontinuous wherever cos x = 0.
A function formed by adding, multiplying, or composing continuous functions is continuous everywhere all of its component pieces are continuous.
A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of the interval. On a closed interval the endpoints require only one-sided continuity matching the function value.

To make a piecewise function continuous by choosing an unknown constant, set the left-hand limit equal to the right-hand limit equal to the function value at the seam where the rule changes, then solve for the constant.

A piecewise function can only be discontinuous at the seams where its rule changes, because each individual piece is typically a continuous function on its own. Continuity therefore reduces to matching pieces at those boundary points.
Example of finding a constant for continuity: if f(x) = x² + k for x ≤ 3 and f(x) = 2x + 1 for x > 3, setting 9 + k = 7 gives k = -2, which welds the pieces together at (3, 7) with no jump.

If a problem requires a piecewise function to be both continuous and differentiable and gives two unknown constants, two equations are needed: one from matching values (continuity) and one from matching derivatives (differentiability).

Differentiability requires continuity: if a function is differentiable at a point it must be continuous there, but a continuous function need not be differentiable, such as the absolute value function which has a corner at x = 0.

Continuity is the required hypothesis for the major theorems of calculus, including the Intermediate Value Theorem, the Extreme Value Theorem, the Mean Value Theorem, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.
